torch.name: Torch
torch.lore: A stick of pine with one end wrapped in rags soaked in pitch: the light that soldiers, miners and grave-robbers carried for thousands of years. It burns smoky and orange for an hour or so, and then it is ash. It shows you the room, and it shows you to everything in the room.

horn_lantern.name: Horn Lantern
horn_lantern.lore: A tin frame with windows of cow horn, scraped so thin that the light shines through. The English called it a lanthorn, and the old spelling remembers the horn. It burns lamp oil, the horn keeps the wind off the flame, and it throws a steadier light than any torch.

dark_lantern.name: Dark Lantern
dark_lantern.lore: A lantern with a single window and a sliding iron shutter, made for watchmen and for thieves. Its light goes forward in a beam, where you point it, and little of it spills back toward whoever is watching. On the night of 4 November 1605 Guy Fawkes was arrested in a cellar under the House of Lords with a dark lantern in his hand. It is still kept in the Ashmolean Museum at Oxford.

everburning_lamp.name: Everburning Lamp
everburning_lamp.lore: Old writers tell of lamps found still burning in sealed tombs. Saint Augustine wrote of a lamp in a temple of Venus that no wind or rain could put out. In 1485 workmen on the Appian Way opened a Roman tomb said to hold Tullia, the daughter of Cicero, and the story grew that a lamp was burning beside her after fifteen hundred years. The alchemists spent centuries trying to make one. This one needs no oil.

jacks_lantern.name: Jack's Lantern
jacks_lantern.unidentified_name: a hollowed turnip with a coal glowing inside
jacks_lantern.lore: The Irish tell of Stingy Jack, a drunkard who tricked the Devil twice and made him promise never to take his soul. When Jack died, Heaven would not have him, and the Devil kept his word and would not let him into Hell either. He threw Jack one ember of hellfire to see his way by, and Jack carried it in a hollowed turnip, and he walks the dark roads with it still. Irish children carved turnip lanterns on All Hallows' Eve to keep him away; in America they used pumpkins. A coal from Hell does not go out.

psyches_lamp.name: Psyche's Lamp
psyches_lamp.unidentified_name: a small clay oil lamp, its spout blackened
psyches_lamp.lore: In the story Apuleius tells, Psyche married a husband who came to her only in the dark and forbade her ever to see his face. Her sisters told her he was a monster. One night she filled a lamp, lit it and held it over him as he slept, and saw that he was the god Cupid himself. A drop of hot oil fell from the lamp onto his shoulder, and he woke and fled from her. By its light, what hides from sight is seen.

heros_lamp.name: Hero's Lamp
heros_lamp.unidentified_name: a bronze lamp on a chain, made to hang in a window
heros_lamp.lore: Hero was a priestess of Aphrodite at Sestos, and Leander loved her from Abydos, across the strait of the Hellespont. Every night she lit a lamp in the window of her tower, and he swam the strait toward it, and before dawn he swam home again. One winter night a storm blew the lamp out, Leander lost his way in the dark water and drowned, and Hero threw herself from her tower. The poet Musaeus told the story. In 1810 Lord Byron swam the Hellespont to prove that it could be done.

hecates_torch.name: Hecate's Torch
hecates_torch.unidentified_name: a black torch with a pale flame that gives no smoke
hecates_torch.lore: Hecate is the goddess of crossroads, of doorways and of the night, and the Greeks showed her with a torch in each hand. When Hades carried Persephone down to the Underworld, Hecate heard her cry. The Homeric Hymn to Demeter tells how she met the grieving mother with a light in her hands and went with her to learn what had happened. Afterwards she stayed beside Persephone in the Underworld. Nothing waits in the dark that her torch does not show.
